captions.text: You have this little boy named Harry who tells
people his name is Bevel.
Well, this story breaks my heart.
He's 5 years old, completely neglected by his hungover,
perpetually partying parents. His babysitter,
Mrs. Connin, takes him out to a rural river
healing. There is a preacher standing waist deep in
the slow red river, singing and preaching to a
crowd. Mhm. He takes this little boy, swings him
upside down, and violently plunges his head into
the water, telling him he now counts.
Later, to escape the miserable, silent neglect of his
parents' apartment, where he's just wandering around, emptying ashtrays
on the rug and watching them sleep off hangovers,
the boy returns to the river He wads in,
trying to baptize himself looking for the kingdom of
Christ the preacher promised him.
He fights the water.
He's choking, but eventually the current catches him like
a long gentle hand and pulls him swiftly forward
and down to his drowning death.
It is horrifying on a literal physical A
neglected child drowns, but spiritually, textually,
the river current catching him like a gentle hand
is the arrival of grace.
Grace is a terrifying physical force that often ends
in death in these stories.
Wait, I have to stop here and really interrogate
this. How on earth is getting shot in the
chest three times by a serial killer or a
neglected 5-year-old drowning alone in a muddy river grace
to a modern listener?
To me, that's just a bleak, horrifying, utterly hopeless
tragedy. It feels like total nihilism masked
as religion. It absolutely feels hopeless if you
were looking at it through our modern secular materialist
lens. Right. Because we value life.
Exactly. Today, we generally believe that the ultimate good
is a long, comfortable, painless physical life.
But to understand this trap, you have to completely
immerse yourself in O'Connor's fiercely strictly orthodox
Catholic Okay. So, how does she see it?
